common_name: Apalachee Pecan (USDA Scab-Resistant Early-Season Small-Nut Pecan)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or containerized grafted trees in late winter while dormant. A Type I (protandrous) pecan, releasing pollen before its own pistillate flowers are receptive, so it needs a Type II pollinator such as Sumner or Moreland planted nearby. Space 50-60 feet apart for full-sized trees.

directions: Apalachee was released by the USDA-ARS Pecan Breeding Program in 2009 from a cross of Moore and Schley made in Brownwood, Texas. It is highly resistant to pecan scab (Fusicladosporium effusum), the dominant disease constraint on Gulf South pecan production, making it a strong low-spray option for home orchards. Nuts are small, roughly 84 per pound, but well filled, with about 54% kernel, and ripen early, about three weeks after Pawnee. As a Type I pollen shedder, plant it with a Type II cultivar for full nut set, and expect a moderate tendency toward alternate bearing common to most early-ripening pecans.
sources: University of Georgia Pecan Breeding Program

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in late winter while dormant. A Type I (protandrous) pecan with pollen shed and pistil receptivity timing similar to Pawnee and Desirable, so pair it with a Type II cultivar such as Oconee or Sumner nearby for reliable pollination. Space 50-60 feet apart for full-sized trees.

directions: Mandan was released by the USDA-ARS Pecan Breeding Program in 2009 from a cross of BW-1 and Osage (tested as USDA 85-1-2), selected for its combination of high scab resistance, late budbreak, and excellent tree strength. Nut maturity is very early, about a week ahead of Pawnee, producing a large, high-quality nut with a good proportion of halves and large pieces suitable for the retail trade. Mandan is a Type I pollen shedder and needs a Type II pollinator planted nearby, and its high scab resistance makes it a good low-input choice for humid Gulf South plantings.
sources: University of Georgia Pecan Breeding Program

common_name: Huffman Pecan (UGA Scab-Resistant Desirable Replacement, Large-Nut Pecan)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in full sun with no shade tolerance, should go into new orchard sites rather than being interplanted into older, shaded trees. A Type I (protandrous) pecan and needs a Type II pollinator such as Elliott, Stuart, Schley, or Zinner planted nearby. Space 50-60 feet apart for full-sized trees.

directions: Huffman was released by the University of Georgia in 2012 (Dr. Darrell Sparks) from a cross of Pawnee and Desirable, selected at the UGA Horticulture Farm in Watkinsville as a scab-resistant replacement for Desirable. It produces a very large nut, 37-39 per pound, with 52-55% kernel and Desirable-like shape and color, and its scab resistance is markedly superior to Desirable's in Georgia trials. Huffman thins its own crop similarly to Desirable and needs little additional hand-thinning to bear consistently from year to year. As a Type I pollen shedder, plant it near a Type II cultivar for good nut set.
sources: University of Georgia Pecan Breeding Program

common_name: Whiddon Pecan (UGA Scab-Resistant Cape Fear and Desirable Replacement Pecan)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in full sun; tolerates partial shading somewhat better than Huffman but still performs best in an open orchard setting. A Type I (protandrous) pecan and needs a Type II pollinator such as Elliott, Stuart, or Schley planted nearby. Space 50-60 feet apart for full-sized trees.

directions: Whiddon was released by the University of Georgia in 2015 (Dr. Darrell Sparks) from a cross of Pawnee and Desirable, developed as a replacement for Desirable and Cape Fear in Georgia orchards. It produces a large, slightly oblong nut, about 40 per pound, with 52-54% kernel matching Desirable's color, and its scab resistance is good in well-managed orchards and superior to Desirable's. Whiddon shows a clear alternate bearing pattern, with off-year crops running roughly 50% lighter than on-year crops, so growers should plan for crop thinning in heavy years. As a Type I pollen shedder, pair it with a Type II cultivar for reliable pollination.
sources: University of Georgia Pecan Breeding Program

common_name: Tanner Pecan (UGA Scab-Resistant Early-Harvest Desirable Replacement Pecan)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in full sun; grows into a large tree with a relatively thin canopy. A Type I (protandrous) pecan and is well pollinated by Lakota, a Type II cultivar; space 50-60 feet apart for full-sized trees.

directions: Tanner was released by the University of Georgia in 2015 (Dr. Darrell Sparks) from a cross of Wichita and Pawnee, one of three scab-resistant Desirable replacements developed alongside Huffman and Whiddon. It produces a large, slightly oblong nut, 40-45 per pound, with 52-55% kernel, harvesting early, around September 20 in south Georgia trials, similar to Byrd and Treadwell. Field evaluations describe scab resistance as good in well-cared-for orchards and superior to Desirable's, though testing has been more limited than for the older standard cultivars. Tanner sets relatively few nuts per cluster, which growers report reduces the need for hand-thinning; as a Type I pollen shedder it should be planted with a Type II cultivar such as Lakota nearby.
sources: University of Georgia Pecan Breeding Program

common_name: Seneca Pecan (USDA Compact Cold-Hardy Northern Pecan)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in late winter while dormant. Bred from northern-origin parent trees and needs a compatible pecan cultivar of the opposite pollen-shed type planted nearby for full nut set. Space 50-60 feet apart for full-sized trees.

directions: Seneca was released by the USDA Agricultural Research Service, patented in 2023, from a 1997 cross of two northern-origin selections, NC-2B and NC-4, themselves derived from the classic native pecans Colby and Peruque. It was bred specifically for the northern edge of the pecan range: the tree is compact, breaks bud late in spring, and stops growth early in fall, giving it strong freeze tolerance in regions where standard Gulf South cultivars struggle. Seneca produces high-quality, cream-kerneled nuts early in the season and carries useful resistance to pecan scab. Its size and hardiness make it a good fit for northern gardeners well outside the traditional Gulf Coast pecan belt.

common_name: Warren 346 Pecan (Early-Ripening Scab-Resistant Northern Native Pecan)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in late winter while dormant. A Type I (protandrous) pecan and needs a compatible Type II pollinator planted nearby for good nut set. Space 50-60 feet apart for full-sized trees; watch for powdery mildew rather than scab as the primary disease concern.

directions: Warren 346 was selected from a grove of native pecan trees owned by Dale Warren near Chillicothe, Missouri, and has become a benchmark early-ripening cultivar for northern pecan growing regions. Its defining trait is very early ripening, with shuck split beginning as early as the last week of August and nuts starting to fall free by mid-September, well ahead of most Gulf South cultivars. Nuts are small, about 92 per pound, but well filled at 51% kernel. The tree is notably scab resistant, though it is more susceptible to powdery mildew than many Gulf South cultivars, so watch for that disease instead. As a Type I pollen shedder, plant it with a Type II pollinator nearby.

common_name: Peruque Pecan (Historic Early-Ripening Missouri Native Pecan)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in late winter while dormant. A Type I (protandrous) pecan and needs a compatible Type II pollinator planted nearby for good nut set. Netting or scare devices may be needed at harvest, as the thin-shelled nuts attract crows and jays. Space 50-60 feet apart for full-sized trees.

directions: Peruque was discovered growing wild in the Mississippi River floodplain near St. Charles, Missouri, and was brought to national attention in the 1950s for its precocious, reliably annual bearing habit. It produces a medium-sized, thin-shelled nut, about 80 per pound, that ripens in mid-September, among the earliest of any named pecan, which makes it valuable for far-northern growing regions with short frost-free seasons. Peruque is notably scab-susceptible compared to modern resistant releases, and its thin shell makes the crop a favorite target for crows and jays, so plan on bird deterrence at harvest. As a Type I pollen shedder, it needs a Type II pollinator planted nearby.

common_name: Posey Pecan (Historic Thin-Shelled Indiana Native Pecan)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in late winter while dormant. Needs a compatible pecan cultivar of the opposite pollen-shed type planted nearby for good nut set; it has been grown alongside Kanza in regional trials. Space 50-60 feet apart for full-sized trees.

directions: Posey traces back to a large native pecan tree that grew on the bank of the Wabash River in Gibson County, Indiana, famous in the late 1800s for its large size and thin shell; the named cultivar was propagated from that tree's seedlings in the early 1900s. It is among the thinnest-shelled of the northern-grown pecans, with a distinctively rough, winged shuck and a vigorous, heavy-bearing tree that develops shaggy, hickory-like bark with age. Posey has performed as a large, vigorous grower in regional Kansas and Missouri variety trials alongside Kanza, and has shown only slight scab susceptibility in those far-northern trial sites, though it has not been widely tested under humid Gulf South disease pressure. Match it with a compatible cross-pollinating cultivar of the opposite pollen-shed type for reliable nut set.
sources: Kansas State University Research and Extension

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in late winter while dormant. A Type II (protogynous) pecan and needs a compatible Type I pollinator planted nearby for good nut set. A fungicide program is advisable for scab control in humid climates. Space 50-60 feet apart for full-sized trees.

directions: Colby is a native selection out of Illinois, introduced in 1957 and long used as a benchmark far-northern pecan cultivar for growers well outside the traditional Gulf South range. It produces a medium-large, oval nut, around 60 per pound, roughly 45% kernel, that is notably large for an ultra-northern-adapted variety, though its thicker shell gives a lower kernel percentage than Gulf South standards. Colby is scab susceptible and benefits from a fungicide program where humidity is high; it has also served as a parent of other cold-hardy cultivars such as NC-4. As a Type II pollen shedder, plant it with a Type I pollinator nearby for reliable nut set.
